rationale: A wins because it respects the fact pattern and marks the holes instead of decorating them. Its line, "Linear is betting it can grow into product teams without a sales team," is a little hot, but it immediately demands confirmation; B turns the same thin fact into "Linear is selling to the enterprise without an enterprise sales team," which the update does not support. B also drags in "Jira, Asana, Notion, and Monday" and "incumbents own" as if the brief supplied a competitive map. That is not strategy; that is a confident hallucination wearing a blazer.
gaps_in_A: "Linear is betting it can grow into product teams without a sales team" overstates the supplied fact. The update says no enterprise sales team is mentioned, not that Linear has none.

"The prevailing belief in that beat is that moving from a single-function tool to a cross-functional platform requires enterprise sales headcount" is plausible, but still unsupported by the update. It belongs as a hypothesis unless sourced.
"the only one grounded enough to pitch now" is a bit too generous. The category angle still needs the concrete before/after product capability and visuals before a serious reporter bites.
gaps_in_B: "Jira, Asana, Notion, and Monday" and "contested ground the incumbents own" invent a competitive map the update did not provide. A reporter may think that; this brief does not prove it.

"Linear is selling to the enterprise without an enterprise sales team" is the biggest foul. The launch expands to product managers and designers; it does not say enterprise, whole-org buying, or no sales team.

"product, design, and stakeholder buyers" turns stakeholder views into stakeholder buyers. The update says the product has stakeholder views aimed at PMs and designers, not that stakeholders are a buyer segment.
"the slower, more visual, more collaborative way non-engineers work" may be a smart tension, but it is asserted as category truth without evidence. Keep it as a question, not a premise.
